analysis.one_liner: Makes new national monuments expire after six months unless Congress votes to keep them.
analysis.headline: The bill would have made new national monuments expire after six months unless Congress extended them; it died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Antiquities Act, a president can declare federal land a national monument without Congress acting. This bill would change that: any new monument designation would automatically expire six months later — or at the end of the current Congress — unless Congress passed a law to keep it. If Congress let it lapse, that land could not be turned into a monument again for 25 years. Supporters say this returns land-use decisions to elected lawmakers; critics say it effectively ends presidents' ability to protect public land from development, mining, and drilling.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries and state officials who want fewer permanent land-use restrictions — mining, drilling, ranching, and off-road interests on federal land in the West — gain, because monument designations lock in protections against development, and this bill would make those protections temporary and reversible. Presidents and would-be monument advocates lose the ability to protect land on their own.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Extractive and grazing interests on federal land

how_it_helps.text: It would give Congress, rather than the president, the final say over whether a national monument becomes permanent: a designation would lapse after six months or the end of the sitting Congress unless extended by statute [S2].
If Congress let a monument lapse, the same land could not be re-designated as a monument for 25 years, which would prevent a future president from simply re-designating it [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the cost where a monument would have protected archaeological sites, sacred landscapes, habitat, or recreation areas from industrial development — and future generations could not recover the designation for 25 years after a lapse. Presidents lose a conservation tool they have had since 1906.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public that uses and values protected lands

drawbacks.text: The six-month sunset would make presidential monument protection largely symbolic: without a willing Congress acting quickly, a new monument would expire and the land could not be re-protected for 25 years.

The same limitation applies to any president, so a future administration sympathetic to conservation could not protect archaeological sites, sacred landscapes, or rare habitat without Congress agreeing — removing a check that has existed since 1906.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real grievance — large-scale monument designations can restrict grazing, off-road use, and development on land residents use — but it does so by sunsetting all monument protections after six months unless Congress affirmatively extends them, something a divided Congress rarely does. That effectively ends unilateral public-land protection and hands the decision to Congress, where local industry pressure is strongest. The cost to the public (losing a century-old protection mechanism for archaeological sites and landscapes) outweighs the gain in legislative control.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 14, 2023, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S4].
No further action was taken — no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S4].
Only five senators cosponsored the bill, all Republicans [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Presidential monument authority remains intact, so conservation and outdoor-recreation interests keep the current protection tool. Extractive industries and their Senate backers did not get the 25-year re-designation ban they sought, but they face no new restrictions either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Presidential monument authority and conservation groups

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee

for.name: Sens. Romney, Risch, Sullivan, and Cruz

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill got no hearing in the Democratic-controlled Senate before the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Mining, oil, gas, and grazing interests on federal land
industries.note: New national monuments can restrict mining, drilling, and grazing on public land. A six-month sunset with a 25-year re-designation ban would keep those uses open. The bill's interests run against permanent public-land protection, which the public cannot easily recreate once lost.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and tourism economies near monuments
industries.note: Monument designations often boost tourism, camping, and gateway-town economies; expiring designations would create uncertainty for these businesses, though they are not a party to the bill.

industries.industry: Conservation organizations and tribal nations seeking monument protection
industries.note: Tribes and conservation groups have used the Antiquities Act process to protect sacred sites and habitat; the bill removes the main tool that works without congressional action.
